query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA, exposure to elevated-temperature oxidizing atmospheres accelerates the transformation and coarsening of the initially fine Cr- and Ti-rich nitride/σ precipitates by promoting interfacial oxidation at grain boundaries. This oxidation creates brittle oxide layers that reduce inter-granular cohesion and trigger catastrophic failure, whereas reducing environments mitigate this transformation.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-printed, supersaturated single-phase FCC structure containing fine metastable nitride and σ phase precipitates formed during selective laser melting.
generation.intervention: Substitute the gas environment by systematically varying the oxygen partial pressure (i.e. comparing oxidizing vs reducing atmospheres) during high-temperature exposure.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures between approximately 900 K and 1300 K with controlled exposure durations in atmospheres differing primarily in oxygen content.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation and growth of Cr/Ti-rich oxide layers at precipitate/matrix interfaces and along grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: In an oxidizing atmosphere, oxygen reacts at the interfaces of the metastable precipitates and grain boundaries, causing accelerated coarsening and conversion of precipitates into brittle oxide phases. This interfacial oxidation undermines grain cohesion, leading to embrittlement and ultimately catastrophic failure. Under reducing conditions, this oxidation-driven transformation is suppressed, preserving the ductile FCC matrix.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples exposed to oxidizing conditions will exhibit increased intergranular oxidation, coarsened precipitate morphologies, and a decline in ductility (e.g. increased microhardness but lower fracture toughness) relative to the as-printed baseline. Conversely, samples in reducing atmospheres should show slower or reduced oxidation with less degradation of mechanical properties.
generation.baseline: The as-manufactured HEA displaying a fine dispersion of nitrides/σ phases within a homogeneous FCC matrix with favorable mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: Effects are anticipated during prolonged exposure at high temperatures (900–1300 K) with environmental control of oxygen levels being critical; results may differ outside these conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of oxidation-induced precipitate transformation and the threshold oxygen partial pressures required to trigger catastrophic failure remain to be quantified. Additional microstructural studies are needed to resolve the interplay between oxidation and decomposition of metastable precipitates in this specific alloy.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple batches of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 samples. Expose one group to a controlled oxidizing atmosphere (e.g. air or oxygen-rich gas) and a second group to a reducing atmosphere (e.g. inert gas with a low oxygen partial pressure) at temperatures between 900 K and 1300 K for identical time intervals. After exposure, perform detailed microstructural characterization (using SEM/TEM and XRD) to assess the presence and extent of oxide formation at precipitate boundaries, and mechanical testing (microhardness and fracture toughness tests) to evaluate changes in mechanical behavior.
measurements: Quantitative analysis of oxide layer thickness and distribution along grain boundaries and around precipitates
Measurement of precipitate size and morphology changes via microscopy
Mechanical properties (microhardness, fracture toughness) relative to the baseline as-printed state
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant differences are observed in oxide formation, precipitate coarsening, or mechanical degradation between the oxidizing and reducing environments despite identical exposure conditions, then the hypothesis—that oxidation-mediated precipitate transformation governs degradation and catastrophic failure—would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Meanwhile, the corrosion behavior of the Cr18Mn27Fe27.5Ni27.5 high entropy alloy seems to follow mechanisms observed in conventional alloys, which is controlled by the thermodynamic stability of corrosion products relative to fluorine potential and the level of impurities in the salt. Similar results were observed during the corrosion of CrFeNiCo, CrFeNiCoMn, and CrFeNiCuMn high entropy systems in various aqueous solutions. That being said, it is not sufficient to draw conclusions about the role of the high entropy of mixing and sluggish diffusion in the corrosion behavior of HEAs. More experimental results with various HEAs in different salt media would be needed to better understand the behavior of HEAs in these corrosive environments.

The high entropy alloy (HEA) of equiatomic composition CrNiFeCoMn and with FCC crystal structure was additively manufactured in a selective laser melting (SLM) process starting from mechanically alloyed powders. The as-produced alloy shows fine nitride and σ phase precipitates, which are Cr-rich and stable up to about 900 K. The precipitates increase in number and dimensions after long-period annealing at 900–1300 K, with a change in the HEA mechanical properties. Higher aging temperatures in the furnace, above 1300 K, turn the alloy into a single FCC structure, with the disappearance of the nitride and σ phase precipitates inside the grains and at the grain boundaries, but still with the presence of a finer Cr-rich nitride precipitation phase. These results suggest that the as-produced HEA is a supersaturated solid solution at low and intermediate temperature with nitrides and σ nanostructures.

For a CrCoMnFeNi alloy to be used in industrial applications, it is critical to investigate both the behavior of this HEA during prolonged use at high temperature and the manufacturing process, not to mention an accurate investigation into the microstructural evolution. In fact, precipitates could lead to relevant changes in the alloy’s mechanical properties, either increasing the strength or embrittling the alloy. In both cases it is important to control the new phase precipitation or dissolution upon heat treatment. Moreover, the kinetics and the mechanisms of a second phase precipitation into FCC HEAs are still poorly understood and this spurred us to further investigate them. Furthermore, it is proved that the secondary phases may contribute significantly to the HEAs’ properties, and it was reported that HEAs can overcome the strength-ductility trade-off when containing two or more phases [,].
